name: Lighting / smiling side meta

lead: This meta combines choosing which side of the face to show, using lighting that flatters it, and practising an even smile. People use it to look more symmetrical and attractive in photos and in person, and the change shows right away in the resulting photo.

Light direction changes how light and shadow fall across the face, and an even smile equalises how far each mouth corner lifts. Research on smile symmetry exists in dental and surgical settings, but no study has tested these tactics as practised.

paras: People test sides and light directions, such as soft light from the front or a window to one side, and practise smiling in a mirror to even out the mouth corners, then reuse the setup that works for them.
No documented harms are reported for the practice itself.

chain: Light it well, even out the smile
angle.text: Side choice, lighting direction and a deliberately even smile make the face look more symmetrical and attractive on camera and in person. The visual change is immediate in the resulting photo.

lead: The lighting and smiling side meta is a set of photo-and-presentation tactics in looksmaxxing circles: which side of the face to show a camera, how light falls on it, and how evenly a person smiles. Followers use it to look more symmetrical, better defined and more attractive in photographs and in person. A well-chosen side and light can even out skin tone and bring out bone structure, and a practised smile can make the mouth corners lift more evenly.

The practice has two overlapping halves. Lighting tactics cover the direction, softness and colour temperature of light, and forum users on looksmax.org debate daylight versus indoor bulbs and the use of window light for rating photos [1][2][3]. Smile tactics cover picking a more flattering side and mirror practice so that a smile looks less lopsided.

Photographers describe named lighting set-ups such as loop, butterfly, split and Rembrandt lighting that change how a face reads, and guides for non-professionals recommend soft, large light sources over small hard ones [4]. Psychology research has documented a tendency to pose and to prefer the left cheek in portraits [5][6], and dental and surgical literature examines smile symmetry [7][8][9][10][11]. Close camera distance is also known to distort facial proportions [12][13], and Duchenne's smile distinction is well documented [14]. No published study has tested the combined practice as followers describe it.

paras: Proponents describe the meta as having two linked parts. The first is choosing a preferred side of the face to present and arranging light so that shadows and highlights favour it. The second is smile training: practising in a mirror so that both mouth corners rise by a similar amount, or so that a smile looks less lopsided.

The idea of a 'good side' rests on the observation that most faces are not perfectly symmetrical, so a photo from one angle can show a straighter jaw line, a higher cheekbone or a more even eye area than the other. Users compare photos of the same face from each side and under different light before settling on a profile picture or a pose.

Lighting threads on looksmax.org are a long-running part of the discussion. One early thread opens with the observation that many people call direct sunlight the best way to judge a photo, while most real-life settings such as school or clubs use indoor light [1]. One reply distinguishes outdoor shade from indoor screen light, and another states that lower colour temperatures of about 2700 to 3000 K make skin look better than 4000 to 5000 K white light, citing a reviewer who films in a garden at night because fluorescent light washed out his skin [1].

Other threads ask whether lighting matters a great deal, whether a particular light shows the 'truth', and whether leaning on lighting is itself a 'cope' or 'fraud' [2][3][15][16]. Rating threads specify the light, such as natural light with no filter, window light or club-style light, because members consider the same face to rate differently under each [17][18]. A further thread examines how a recessed or forward infraorbital area looks under harsh light [19], and one post asks whether a contour that appears on the cheek in certain light at higher body fat suggests hollow cheeks at lower body fat [20].

Photographers describe a small set of named portrait set-ups. In loop lighting a small nose shadow falls on the shadow side of the face; butterfly lighting puts the main light above and in line with the camera, giving a butterfly-shaped shadow under the nose; split lighting places the light about 90 degrees to the side so half the face is lit; and Rembrandt lighting uses a light high and to one side that leaves a patch of light on the far cheek.

The key light sets the highlight modelling, the fill light controls how dark the shadows are, and the distance of the lights from the face sets how fast shadows transition from light to dark. Wikipedia notes that light direction supplies cues to shape, so the same face can look rounder or flatter depending on where highlights and shadows fall. A 2020 Popular Science guide says large light sources such as a big window give soft shadows, small direct sources give hard-edged ones that emphasise wrinkles and blemishes, and low sun near sunrise and sunset gives a warmer, softer light [4]. This is the mechanism forum members refer to when they say harsh overhead light hollows the eye area or that side light brings out bone structure [19].

Wikipedia reports that faces are on average slightly offset to the left relative to the ears, so the right side appears larger, by roughly 2 degrees at birth and about 0.5 degrees in adults. Work by Rhodes and colleagues in 1998 found that more symmetrical faces were rated more attractive, with a larger effect for female faces, while Perrett and colleagues in 1999 found that symmetrising older faces tended to raise attractiveness but symmetrising young faces tended to lower it. The same article cautions that mirroring face halves creates artificial features, and reports that about 76 percent of people show greater mouth movement on the right side during speech.

Separate research looks at which cheek people show. A 2012 study by Kelsey Blackburn and James Schirillo of Wake Forest University, published in Experimental Brain Research, found participants rated the left side of faces as more pleasant, including in mirror-reversed images, and the authors proposed that the left cheek shows greater emotional intensity [5]. A review in the BC Medical Journal traces the left-cheek bias in portraits to a 1973 analysis of 1,474 paintings, in which women were posed left-cheek-forward 68 percent of the time and men 56 percent, and reports the bias in selfies and Instagram photos; it adds that the same review found no cheek bias in web portraits of physicians and surgeons [6].

Smile practice in the community usually means standing in front of a mirror and rehearsing a smile in which both mouth corners rise by a similar amount, so that one side does not sit higher or show more teeth. Users also pick the side from which the smile looks best. No standard protocol exists, and no trial of mirror training for smile evenness has been published.

Photographers note that apparent facial proportions change with the distance between camera and subject. A wide-angle lens used at close range can make the nose look large relative to the rest of the face and can distort expression, whereas a longer lens from farther away flattens features; focal lengths of about 85 to 135 mm on a 35 mm camera are generally treated as flattering for portraits [12]. The effect comes from camera distance rather than the lens as such [12].

A 2018 paper in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery by Boris Paskhover of Rutgers New Jersey Medical School and Stanford computer scientists built a mathematical model using average head measurements. Press coverage reported that a selfie taken about 12 inches from the face makes the base of the nose look about 30 percent wider and the tip about 7 percent wider than a portrait from 5 feet [13]. Paskhover described a selfie as 'in essence looking into a portable funhouse mirror,' and said more research is needed on whether this distortion drives people to seek cosmetic surgery [13]. Looksmaxxing users who compare face photos often specify the camera distance and lens for this reason.

The French neurologist Guillaume Duchenne distinguished two kinds of smile in the mid-nineteenth century. A Duchenne smile contracts both the zygomatic major and the orbicularis oculi, lifting the cheeks and creating crow's feet, and is sometimes called smiling with the eyes; a smile using the zygomatic major alone is the voluntary 'Pan Am' smile [14]. Messinger and colleagues reported in 2001 that the eye-involving form is uniquely associated with positive emotion [14].

Smiling tends to make people seem more likable and approachable, according to a 2002 study by Gladstone, while a 2016 study by Krys and colleagues found cultural differences in how smiles are read, with smiling individuals judged as less intelligent in some cultures [14]. Smile frequency in posed photographs also varies by country [14]. Wikipedia notes that chronic Botox use around the eyes can paralyse the muscles needed for a Duchenne smile [14]. These findings inform how followers think about showing teeth, eye involvement and which side of the smile to favour, though they do not test side or lighting choices.

sections.h: Smile symmetry in dental and surgical research
paras: Dental researchers have studied how common smile asymmetry is and how smile features relate to perceived attractiveness. A study of an adult population in southern Europe examined the prevalence of alterations in smile symmetry [8], and a 2022 paper reviewed morphological features of smile attractiveness and their relation to perception and gingival aesthetic parameters [7].

A separate surgical literature addresses smile restoration in facial nerve palsy. A study of free-muscle transfer for midface reanimation followed 24 adults for five years or longer at one centre and evaluated smile symmetry and function [9]; a prospective evaluation of free gracilis muscle transfer examined 20 patients with nonflaccid facial paralysis [10]; and other work looks at weakening the depressor anguli oris muscle to improve symmetry in post-paralysis palsy [11]. These treat a medical condition and are not studies of cosmetic smile practice.

No studies found. Studies of smile symmetry in dental populations [7][8] and of surgical smile rehabilitation in facial palsy [9][10][11] exist, as do perception studies of left-cheek preference [5], but none tests lighting choices, side selection for photos or smile training as a looks intervention. The selfie-distortion work is a geometric modelling study rather than a trial of photo outcomes [13].

lore.intro: Lighting and angle are common topics in rating and photo threads on looksmax.org, where members use them both to present themselves and to question how much a photo reveals [1][15][16].
